newsitem.title: USA: US crude outlook-losing steam on Iraq and supplies.
newsitem.headline: US crude outlook-losing steam on Iraq and supplies.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices, blinded by bullish technical sentiment recently, are finally showing some telltale signs of weakness as Iraqi oil sales and ample supplies bear down, traders and analysts said Monday.
The softer backwardation in the West Texas Intermediate nearby spread, currently at 43 cents, down from 80-90 cents two months ago, also signals a turnaround in direction.
"The whole things smells like it's losing steam, because of Iraq and no more strength on the buying side for wets," a U.S. cash crude trader said.
Crude markets, long in defiance of fundamentals, charged up to its highest levels at $23.35 a barrel last week for September, ahead of the NYMEX contract's expiration Tuesday.
NYMEX October light crude futures finished on Friday at $21.96 a barrel, correcting on its sharp gains, but appears likely to ease this week as supply fears take precedence.
The Atlantic arbitrage, meanwhile, has opened the window to North Sea Gullfaks and Oseberg, with Brent also offered for September although domestic grades stayed competitive.
Latin American spot cargoes also made their way into the U.S. Gulf, along with rare Russian Urals.
The sale of Urals into Cuba by a trader for late September reflected growing pressure on Mediterranean margins and concerns about limited Iraqi crude oil sales.

"Most expectations about Iraq have floated through the market, but sales will bring on some downward psychology adjustment," Charles McSpadden, vice-president of market analysis for Bonner & Moore said.
Products are also expected to take a toll on crude demand, despite low middle distillate stocks.
"We're into the season where gasoline loses margins. It's 50 percent of the refined products barrel," McSpadden said.

In the longer-term, Tosco reaching a tentative pact with Marcus Hook, Pa. refinery workers towards the reopening of the 172,000 barrel per day (bpd) refinery, announced on Monday, was seen further dragging down gasoline.
Traders said heating oil remains the salvation for high refinery output in the 4Q, but this could be tempered by drought this season cutting into agricultural diesel demand.

Price support this week could surface, however, from hurricane activity, where Edouard packing 130 miles-per-hour (210 kph) winds, could pose a threat to U.S. shipping in the Caribbean and eastern seaboard refineries.
